title: Can return journeys predict boundary occupation?
question: Can depth-crossing dynamics explain kappa on fresh starts, larger territories and unseen rule families?
hypothesis: A local field-dependent crossing model may compose into a return law whose amplitudes set occupation and whose scaling predicts drift.
finding: P2 failed (median relative error 1.07 against 0.20; worse than persistence). P1, P3 and P4 uninformative after a registered second stage (failed tail calibration; no rule-conditional model; radius-4 contexts too sparse); on-disk checkpoint gate met. Boundary dwell E[D] is flat over a 4x range of scale (post hoc, 46 rules); E[T] tracking A/P is then the renewal identity, not a mechanism. Frozen protocol, 768 runs, 46 of 48 rules eligible.
caveat: Prediction criteria and decision rules were frozen before the run; calibration controls partly failed and are reported. Pilot outcomes were inspected before the freeze; two drifting rules never reached the large sizes; analysis reproducible to ~1e-15 only.

title: What does a new cell cost?
question: Can compressed phase memory reproduce the boundary birth process, beyond its mean cost?
hypothesis: Physical excursion duration might explain why close total costs coexist with failed physical-return budgets.
finding: All compressed fields fail native return-budget and waiting-process criteria too; physical-time stretching alone cannot rescue them. All forty prior ant summaries replay exactly.
caveat: Four inspected pilot rules, two seeds and early windows; no universal memory bound. Main outcomes remain unopened. A single coupled phase edit is proposed but unrun.

title: Which parts of an ant’s world keep it close to home?
question: Some ants repeatedly return to a small home region. Is that behaviour stored in particular patches of the colour pattern they have written?
hypothesis: If a patch carries the tether, scrambling it should reduce returns home more than changing a comparable random patch.
finding: The knockout maps identify small sensitive regions in the two hard tethered rules. Later experiments investigate their colours, age and individual cells.
caveat: Sensitivity identifies where an intervention matters; it does not explain how the intact pattern guides a return.

title: Why do some ants spend more time at the edge?
question: Two ants can have similar territory shapes yet spend different amounts of time near fresh ground. Can simple rule features predict that difference?
hypothesis: The boundary occupation factor, kappa, might be set by letter balance, early letters or the mixture of colours at the edge.
finding: Kappa varies reproducibly between rules, but these simple predictors did not explain it in the original analysis. The proposed half-plane mechanism was not built.
caveat: This is an early negative result. Later prefix and growth-control experiments refine the question; it does not rule out every predictor of kappa.

title: Does the perimeter eventually behave like a smooth boundary?
question: A compact two-dimensional territory should have a perimeter proportional to the square root of its area. Is the measured excess a temporary effect?
hypothesis: Longer rotor-walker runs should move the perimeter-versus-area exponent toward one half rather than a larger limiting value.
finding: The late rotor estimate favours one half. This supplies a useful control for the ants, whose measurements approach the limit less cleanly.
caveat: The conclusion relies heavily on the final measured octave. It is numerical evidence, not a proof of the limiting exponent.

title: Why do the visit counts form a cone?
question: Ants revisit the centre of their territory more than its edge. Does that radial profile reveal a special return mechanism?
hypothesis: A cone-shaped accumulated visit profile can follow simply from uniform occupation of a growing territory and its growth exponent.
finding: The cone can be derived under those assumptions. A random-background control correctly fails to follow it, limiting its applicability to the blank-board regime.
caveat: An accumulated cone does not by itself demonstrate uniform instantaneous occupation or explain the growth exponent. The planned square-root turmite control was not run.

title: Why is the ant’s edge broader than the rotor’s?
question: Ant and rotor territories can grow at similar rates while their boundaries fluctuate differently. Does the difference disappear in longer runs?
hypothesis: The ant’s boundary-width exponent might drift toward the rotor’s value as the territory grows.
finding: The gap persists through the extended measurement windows: ants retain broader boundary fluctuations than the rotor under this estimator.
caveat: Boundary width mixes shape and local roughness. The later hull experiments separate these more carefully.

title: Can a rule’s letters tell us what its home will look like?
question: Many tethered ants fall into a small collection of similar home behaviours. Can a simple property of the rule label those groups?
hypothesis: A single rule feature might distinguish each home cluster.
finding: Only a minority of the examined clusters were separable by a single feature, so the proposed general labelling rule failed.
caveat: Failure of single-feature labels does not exclude a combination of features or a dynamical explanation.

title: Does a tether repair damage to its own pattern?
question: Rare colours are unusually important in tethered territories. Are they important because the ant repeatedly repairs damage there?
hypothesis: Frequently visited cells should recover from corruption more readily than less visited cells.
finding: The prediction reverses: damaging the most visited cells hurts most. Rare colours are associated with tethering, but the proposed self-healing mechanism failed.
caveat: Colour and visit frequency are related. Matched comparisons help distinguish them without fully identifying the mechanism.

title: Can rare breakouts dominate an average?
question: For rule RRLLLLLLR, does changing a small starting patch eventually cease to matter, or do rare trajectories keep the growth coefficient variable?
hypothesis: The scaled territory area might settle to a seed-independent coefficient as time grows.
finding: The bulk of trajectories settles much more than early measurements suggested, but rare large breakouts disrupt the moments. A stable-looking typical trajectory can coexist with unstable averages.
caveat: Long-run samples become smaller and rare events are poorly counted. Typical behaviour and mean behaviour must be reported separately.

title: Does depletion inside the territory set boundary access?
question: Could a shortage of visits in part of the interior explain why different rules reach fresh ground at different rates?
hypothesis: Controlled walker variants and matched rule pairs should connect an interior-depletion statistic to kappa, the normalized time at the boundary.
finding: The matched-pair comparison does not consistently order the depletion statistic by kappa. This avenue did not provide the proposed simple explanation.
caveat: The controls perturb more than one aspect of the walk, and not every run supplied a usable fitted window.

title: Is cube-root growth really shared by different ants?
question: Many chaotic ants appear to grow in width like the cube root of time. Do their apparent differences survive much longer observation?
hypothesis: If the differences are transients, long-run ant exponents should approach the rotor control rather than settle at distinct values.
finding: Under the revised, well-posed comparison, all evaluable ants match the rotor at the late window. RLRLLL instead breaks out into a different growth structure.
caveat: Matching a finite-window control does not establish an exact asymptotic exponent. Escapes and changes of regime are part of the result.

title: How much of the exponent spread belongs to the rule?
question: The census shows a distribution of growth exponents. Is that mostly a difference between rules, or variation between starting patterns?
hypothesis: Repeated starts can separate persistent rule differences from seed-to-seed and finite-time variation.
finding: Width-exponent variation has a modest rule-level component under both patched and sparse-background starts; area exponents retain more between-rule structure.
caveat: Width and area need not tell the same story when filling fraction and shape change. The windows remain finite.

title: Does the cube-root pattern survive longer instructions?
question: The first census concentrates on short rules. Does the growth pattern persist when an ant has many more colours to cycle through?
hypothesis: Longer sampled rules should retain a width exponent near one third, while the balance of slow and compact growers may change.
finding: The sampled rule lengths retain exponents near one third. The fraction of very slow growers decreases with length.
caveat: Sampling longer rules is not an exhaustive census, and a finite run cannot certify permanent chaotic growth.

title: The missing ants were slow, not fast
question: Some rules were excluded because the growth fit could not be computed. Were fast-growing ants escaping the board and disappearing from the analysis?
hypothesis: A larger-board rerun should recover unusually fast growth if board escape caused the missing fits.
finding: None of the 153 rules escaped. All had a window with no new cells: the missing fits were stalled or very slow growth, contradicting the proposed explanation.
caveat: This resolves that particular set of missing fits. Other kinds of census exclusion still need their own audit.

title: How often does apparent chaos turn into a highway?
question: An ant can wander for billions of steps before finding a repeating path that carries it away. Does the chance of that late switch stay constant per decade of time?
hypothesis: Extending surviving rules by another decade should produce a similar fraction of new highways if the onset tail remains flat.
finding: The new-highway count falls below the flat-rate prediction. The observed tail thins, while some board escapes still have no classified highway.
caveat: One more decade cannot show whether every survivor eventually switches. Board escape is not itself evidence of a highway.

title: What happens when the rotor’s world has a preferred direction?
question: The rotor walker is a comparison model with arrows stored on the grid. Does biasing those initial arrows destroy cube-root growth?
hypothesis: The alternatives are a continuous change with bias or a range of biases that preserves the exponent before a crossover.
finding: With adequate board size the width exponent persists through moderate bias, then becomes ballistic at stronger bias. Area and shape respond earlier.
caveat: An initial apparent failure was a board-size effect. Width alone can hide elongation and changing area growth.

title: Does the edge settle into a stable colour mixture?
question: The ant sees young colours near fresh ground. Does their mixture stabilize enough to support a time-independent growth description?
hypothesis: Boundary colour shares should become nearly constant over successive late windows.
finding: Larger boundary samples support approximate stability at the percent scale, but the strict fraction-within-tolerance criterion remains inconclusive against the sampling floor.
caveat: Sampling noise matters at the same scale as the proposed drift. Approximate stability is not exact stationarity.

title: Can we trust the growth measurements?
question: A fitted exponent can look convincing even when the observation window is biased. How do our instruments behave on walkers with known comparison behaviour?
hypothesis: A rotor walker should recover cube-root radius growth, while a random walk supplies a different-growth negative control.
finding: The calibration records the finite-window behaviour of the growth, perimeter and shape estimators. It is the reference against which ant fits are judged.
caveat: An estimator that works on the rotor is not automatically unbiased on every ant. Changed windows and estimators require fresh calibration.

title: Can changing one square loosen the tether?
question: After sensitive patches have been found, does the ant’s return behaviour depend on individual cells within them?
hypothesis: Recolouring particular cells should cause greater loss of home returns than recolouring random visited cells.
finding: The fine scan finds individual cells with effects exceeding the random-cell control. Patch-level sensitivity can therefore be localized more precisely.
caveat: Cells were selected from already sensitive regions. This is a targeted follow-up, not an unbiased census of all cells.

title: A census of the worlds ants build
question: What kinds of long-run behaviour emerge when we enumerate short left/right rules instead of choosing a few attractive examples?
hypothesis: The census asks whether recurrent compact growth is common and which rules instead build repeating escape paths or grow very slowly.
finding: The sweep supplies the rule catalogue used by later growth and highway studies. Exact repeats of shorter rules can be removed without changing the main growth summary appreciably.
caveat: Classifications are bounded by the run budget and board size. A rule that has not built a highway yet is not proved never to build one.

title: Which colours occupy the interior and the edge?
question: Colours record visit counts modulo the rule length. Are their spatial mixtures uniform, or does the edge retain a distinct signature?
hypothesis: Repeated visits may mix interior colours while newly reached cells concentrate low colours at the boundary.
finding: The saved tables separate overall, visited and boundary colour statistics, supplying inputs to the tether and edge-colour investigations.
caveat: A colour histogram loses spatial arrangement and cannot by itself establish mixing or explain a return path.

title: Why do some stateful ants grow a different way?
question: Adding an internal state produces many walkers with square-root-like area growth. Are they compact territories with a new exponent, or thin structures?
hypothesis: A simple transition-table feature might distinguish these walkers from compact cube-root-like growers.
finding: No single table feature cleanly separates the classes. The square-root class instead has increasingly thin, effectively one-dimensional geometry.
caveat: These are screened transition tables, with symmetry duplicates and finite observation times; the result is not a full classification theorem.

title: Does the growth story extend to three dimensions?
question: If revisiting old territory slows a two-dimensional ant, what growth should a related walker show in three dimensions?
hypothesis: The dimensional analogy predicts a linear scale near the fourth root of time and visited volume near time to the three-quarter power.
finding: Longer runs remain close to those predicted powers but retain offsets and a slowly changing filling fraction.
caveat: Agreement within registered bands is not proof of the exact exponents or a transfer of the two-dimensional mechanism.

title: How does noise undo the ant’s slow growth?
question: The ant’s movement is deterministic. If we occasionally replace its prescribed turn, does its territory abruptly become random-walk-like?
hypothesis: The alternatives are a sharp change at a noise threshold or a smooth crossover in the measured growth exponent.
finding: The measured area exponent rises smoothly with noise toward diffusive behaviour. No sharp jump is resolved in the tested windows.
caveat: Only three rules were used, and a fixed observation window can blur a time-dependent crossover. Strong-noise board escapes limit the comparison.

title: Do several ants do more than share the work?
question: What changes when several ants edit the same colour field: the growth law, or mainly how much total stepping has been done?
hypothesis: After comparing equal total numbers of ant moves, multi-ant territory areas should remain close to the single-ant case.
finding: Late area ratios are close to the single-ant comparison, with no systematic trend across the tested ant counts.
caveat: The tested scheduling, rules and time range do not establish equivalence for every interacting-ant system.

title: How much of the pattern can a tether survive losing?
question: Tethered ants stay near home on their own mature colour fields. How gradually does that behaviour disappear as the field is scrambled?
hypothesis: If the tether is stored in the field, preserving larger fractions of the original arrangement should progressively recover confinement.
finding: The dose curves connect heavily scrambled, weakly confining fields to intact, strongly confining ones across the tested field ages.
caveat: A dose curve does not identify the responsible cells. Equal numbers of changed cells can have different effects depending on where and how they are changed.

title: Why are the sensitive patches on one side of home?
question: A tether’s sensitive cells appear in a one-sided lobe. Is that orientation fixed by the rule or inherited from the particular colour field?
hypothesis: Comparing field ages can distinguish a fixed compass preference from a lobe that moves with the field’s history.
finding: Across usable ages the lobe is field-tied rather than rule-fixed. A rotation with the ant’s heading corrected serves as an instrument check.
caveat: The first rotated comparison was invalid because its heading was not rotated. Exact rotational covariance is a check, not an independent mechanism test.

title: Is the sensitive region a real scale or a measuring artefact?
question: Does the apparent size of a tether’s important region merely reflect the radius used to define a return home?
hypothesis: If the scale is intrinsic, changing the measurement radius substantially should change the inferred sensitive radius much less.
finding: The sensitive scale grows much less than the chosen home radius, supporting an intrinsic region rather than simple tracking of the measurement disc.
caveat: This is a result for the tested tethered rules and definitions, not a universal physical length scale.

title: Are the important cells special return routes?
question: Do sensitive patches guide the ant home specifically, or are they simply places the ant visits frequently?
hypothesis: Homeward-path statistics and matched interventions should distinguish return-route importance from general occupancy.
finding: Path counts were too correlated with occupancy to discriminate. A subsequent matched intervention found no leg-direction effect, so that return-path explanation was dropped.
caveat: The observational near-null alone was not decisive; it was the follow-up intervention that supplied the stronger test.

title: Does the manner of damage matter?
question: Is losing the tether determined only by how many rare-colour cells an intervention changes?
hypothesis: Patch damage and colour swaps should follow the same response curve once matched by rare cells changed.
finding: Loss correlates with rare cells changed, but patch and swap curves differ. Counting damaged rare cells alone is not enough.
caveat: Different interventions also change spatial structure differently; the comparison does not isolate a unique causal property.

title: Do other tethered ants have the same weak spots?
question: The first sensitive-patch maps concern only two rules. Do similar small hot regions appear in other tethered ants?
hypothesis: A small fraction of territory should carry disproportionate sensitivity in additional rules.
finding: Several additional maps show small hot regions, but two tight-tether rules have no meaningful hot spots under this test.
caveat: The exceptions matter: localized fragility is not a necessary feature of every tether.

title: When do the important patches become important?
question: Are a mature tether’s sensitive regions already doing the same job early in the trajectory?
hypothesis: If they are permanent return machinery, the same windows should be sensitive in younger colour fields.
finding: The tested windows become hot later and are not comparably sensitive at the earliest age, contradicting the simple permanent-set prediction.
caveat: The early null threshold is stricter, so part of the age contrast may come from detectability.

title: What does it cost to grow one more cell?
question: Territory growth combines time spent at the boundary with the chance of entering fresh ground once there. Which part varies with the rule?
hypothesis: Separating boundary occupation, entry probability and perimeter geometry should clarify the measured growth rate.
finding: Early rule letters strongly predict fresh-ground entry probability. Perimeter measurements also show substantial finite-time drift, making exact exponent claims premature.
caveat: The growth decomposition is accounting. Reconstructing growth from its own factors is not an independent explanation of why those factors take their values.

title: How far does the ant growth pattern travel?
question: Is the observed growth peculiar to one ant on a square grid, or does it recur on other lattices and in related walkers?
hypothesis: Screening other geometries, internal states, noise levels and ant counts should reveal which changes preserve compact slow growth.
finding: The screens find related growth regimes alongside distinct thin structures and noise-driven crossovers. They motivate the more focused extension experiments.
caveat: A broad screen is a way to find questions. Small cohorts, short windows and board escapes limit claims of universality.

title: Does microscopic damage destroy confinement?
question: A deterministic trajectory can change completely after one altered cell. Must its large-scale habit of staying home change too?
hypothesis: If tethering is more robust than the exact path, small perturbations can spread through the field without releasing the ant.
finding: Small changes can produce substantial later field damage while the tested ants remain confined. Much larger perturbations can remove the tether.
caveat: Divergence of paths, damage to the field and loss of confinement are different observables.

title: When does a field learn to confine its ant?
question: A fresh ant moves differently on an old field than on a scrambled copy. At what field age does this difference emerge?
hypothesis: Confinement should strengthen as the colour field matures if spatial organization stores the tether.
finding: The real-field and shuffled-field spreads separate as the saved field ages, supporting a role for accumulated spatial organization.
caveat: Restarting an ant changes its position and heading history. The original trajectory and a fresh restart need not have identical behaviour.

title: Making the frontier questions measurable
question: Which simulation and analysis tools are needed to turn the project’s frontier questions into reproducible tests?
hypothesis: Instrument development here supports later tests; it is not itself a registered physical explanation of ant growth.
finding: This folder preserves the code-patch investigation and its associated working record. Scientific conclusions belong to the experiments that use and calibrate those instruments.
caveat: An available instrument is not a completed measurement or a passed hypothesis test.

title: The ant that stopped growing a blob
question: RLRLLL looks like a compact chaotic grower for billions of steps, then begins sweeping columns. What changes at that late transition?
hypothesis: A local signature combining geometry and growth efficiency might distinguish the new phase and recur in other unexplained escapes.
finding: The signature separates the known phases of RLRLLL. Its column sweep leaves a repeating three-colour wake, but the proposed shared global geometry in other escapes fails the registered test.
caveat: This is one deterministic blank-grid trajectory. Describing the sweep does not explain its trigger, and global board escape does not reveal local anatomy.

title: Is the exponent spread really changing empty space?
question: Two territories can have the same width but different numbers of visited cells. Does changing filling fraction explain why their area exponents differ?
hypothesis: Decomposing area into bounding-box size and filling fraction should separate shape growth from progressive filling.
finding: The saved decomposition measures those contributions rather than treating width and area exponents as interchangeable.
caveat: This is a decomposition of existing trajectories, not a mechanism test. Consult the saved analysis before interpreting any particular rule’s contribution.

title: Can different growth curves be put on one scale?
question: Rules grow territories at different rates. Can rescaling by measured boundary factors bring their growth curves together?
hypothesis: If those factors capture the amplitude differences, scaled trajectories should lie closer to a common curve.
finding: The saved analysis tests a collapse using existing probe data. It is a diagnostic of the growth description rather than an independent prediction.
caveat: Factors extracted from the same growth histories can create agreement through accounting. A successful collapse alone cannot establish a causal mechanism.

title: Waiting longer for the apparent chaos to end
question: How many short rules that survive an initial census later find a repeating escape path?
hypothesis: If late onset remains common, extending unresolved rules to much longer budgets should reveal further highways.
finding: The extended sweeps find new highways as well as escapes without detected periodicity. These are distinct outcomes and are recorded separately.
caveat: Unresolved means unresolved within a finite budget. Leaving the board cannot be treated as proof of a repeating highway.

title: Are rare colours concentrated in the weak spots?
question: The knockout maps identify sensitive patches. Do unusual colour classes help explain why those particular patches matter?
hypothesis: If rare colours carry disproportionate tether information, sensitive tiles should be enriched for them and targeted corruption should matter more.
finding: The hard-rule maps support a rare-colour association and motivate class-targeted interventions. Generalization beyond those maps requires separate tests.
caveat: Rare colour, position and visit frequency covary. Enrichment is not sufficient to identify the return mechanism.

title: Are unusually fast and slow exponents reproducible?
question: The census contains rules far from the central growth-exponent peak. Do they remain unusual under new starting patterns?
hypothesis: Repeated patched starts should distinguish a persistent rule effect from an exceptional trajectory or transient.
finding: The experiment remeasures the selected extreme rules alongside random core controls, retaining seed variation rather than trusting a single fitted slope.
caveat: Selection was based on extreme original estimates, so regression toward the centre is expected. The result is not an unbiased sample of all rules.

title: Testing one third against a calibrated comparison
question: Is the narrow exponent peak evidence that different chaotic rules share exactly the same growth law?
hypothesis: Longer runs over many patched starts should reduce differences if the apparent spread mainly reflects finite-time corrections.
finding: The repeated-start study provides the ensemble data for comparing ants with rotor controls. Review corrections show why an uncalibrated extrapolation was too strong.
caveat: The assumed correction form can move the extrapolated limit. Raw late-window estimates and between-seed variation remain essential.

title: Does a tethered ant’s visited territory keep spreading?
question: An ant may stay close to home most of the time while rare excursions enlarge its historical territory. Which notion of radius captures that distinction?
hypothesis: The radius of gyration of visited cells can behave differently from the ant’s current positional spread.
finding: This analysis records octave-by-octave gyration growth for tethered rules, separating the accumulated territory from moment-to-moment confinement.
caveat: A slowly expanding visited set does not mean the ant spends equal time throughout it. The two kinds of radius answer different questions.

title: Does changing the starting colour change the growth?
question: A rule’s letters can be arranged around a cycle. Does rotating that cycle preserve boundary occupation, or is the first colour special?
hypothesis: If kappa belongs to the cyclic necklace alone, rotations of a rule should have similar values.
finding: Kappa is not simply a necklace property. The distinguished starting colour and fresh-ground dynamics matter.
caveat: The comparison is observational and restricted to the measured compact-growth cohort. Rotation is not a blank-board symmetry.

title: Reading the layers of an ant’s colour field
question: What does the spatial arrangement of colours reveal that an overall histogram misses?
hypothesis: Comparing colour layers can expose structure written by repeated visits, while separating young boundary cells from the older interior.
finding: The saved layer and colour records support inspection of the pattern field and related edge investigations.
caveat: These records are descriptive material. A visible pattern needs an explicit statistic and a control before it can count as a tested mechanism.

title: The ants that barely enlarge their world
question: Why do some rules add territory so slowly while continuing to move almost all the time?
hypothesis: Repeated returns to a home region may distinguish these walkers from the more uniformly exploring compact growers.
finding: This folder preserves the slow-growth cohort used by subsequent tether, corruption and restart experiments.
caveat: A small fitted exponent over a finite window does not prove logarithmic growth forever. Long stalls also make ordinary log-log fits fragile.

title: Can a simpler walker reproduce the ant’s memory?
question: The ant writes information into the grid and later responds to it. Which parts of its growth can simpler memory-based walkers reproduce?
hypothesis: Self-avoidance, attraction and other local-memory rules can serve as competing accounts rather than assuming all memory has the same effect.
finding: The comparison walkers show that adding memory alone is not enough to recover the ant’s growth. Some variants grow differently and attraction can trap the walker.
caveat: A failed toy model rejects that implementation, not every possible memory mechanism. Trapping can make a comparison uninformative.

title: Checking the machinery behind the ant measurements
question: Can the project’s exploratory instruments measure trajectory structure and run large sweeps without changing the walk?
hypothesis: Reference comparisons and targeted diagnostics should establish what the tools measure before interpreting them physically.
finding: This archive collects instrument checks and implementation experiments used by the scientific investigations.
caveat: Tool speed and a suggestive diagnostic are not themselves an explanation of the growth law; each physical use needs its own calibration.

title: How random is the ant inside its own territory?
question: A deterministic ant often looks like a random walker in the interior. Do its colours, turns and short-lag motion support that picture?
hypothesis: Repeated visits may mix local colour states enough to produce approximately diffusive short-time motion.
finding: The mixing diagnostics test local colour, turn and displacement statistics rather than inferring randomness from a picture.
caveat: Short-lag diffusion and colour balance do not establish uniform spatial occupation or explain access to the moving boundary.

title: Where does the ant actually spend its time?
question: A picture of visited cells hides how unevenly the ant uses them. What do occupancy maps reveal about compact growers and tethered rules?
hypothesis: If a field guides repeated returns, visit-density and drift maps should distinguish that behaviour from simply filling the territory.
finding: The saved pages place colour, occupancy and motion summaries side by side for selected rules, making the home-versus-territory distinction visible.
caveat: Accumulated visits mix many ages of the growing territory. A bright centre is not direct evidence of an instantaneous inward force.

title: How much does a small initial disturbance matter?
question: The blank-board ant is deterministic. Does a small random starting patch change its large-scale growth, or mainly the particular path?
hypothesis: Repeating each rule over explicit patch seeds can reveal which growth statistics persist despite a changed early history.
finding: The patched-start datasets supply replicate trajectories for the exponent, shape and boundary studies.
caveat: Patch seeds define a particular perturbation ensemble. They are not independent randomness added continuously to the walk.

title: The ant moves through a world it has written
question: How does the colour field left by an ant affect the motion of an ant started on it later?
hypothesis: If the field stores dynamical information, preserving its arrangement should matter beyond merely preserving the number of cells of each colour.
finding: This investigation supplies pattern-field comparisons used to ask how geometry, colour and confinement interact.
caveat: A mature field plus a fresh position and heading need not reproduce the original ant’s dynamical state.

title: Thousands of rules, one crowded growth peak
question: How broadly does cube-root-like growth occur among generalised Langton’s ants, and what distinguishes slower and faster cases?
hypothesis: A census of width, area and boundary statistics should reveal whether compact growers share a common scaling regime.
finding: Many compact growers cluster near a width exponent of one third. Boundary-entry and occupation factors organize deviations, but do not close the dynamical explanation.
caveat: These are finite-window measurements with classification and fit exclusions. Same-run growth accounting cannot prove the exponent’s mechanism.

title: Is the rougher edge just a faster-growing radius?
question: The ant’s boundary width grows faster in time than the rotor’s. Does the difference survive measuring width against territory radius instead?
hypothesis: If growth speed causes the apparent roughness gap, plotting width against radius should remove it.
finding: The ant remains rougher in radius units as well. The simple growth-speed explanation fails under this comparison.
caveat: The cohorts and finite fitting windows still matter; this does not separate persistent shape from local fluctuations.

title: Does a colour class matter beyond its abundance?
question: Rare colours look important to tethering. Is changing those colours more damaging than changing the same number of arbitrary cells?
hypothesis: Matched-count recolouring can separate the identity of a colour class from the sheer amount of damage.
finding: The saved comparisons measure colour-targeted effects against random-cell controls, complementing the patch knockouts.
caveat: Recolouring and shuffling are different interventions. Spatial position and visit history can still confound a colour-only interpretation.

title: Do chaotic ant territories become round?
question: If the growth exponent is shared, do the territories also converge to a common shape and visit-density profile?
hypothesis: Anisotropy should diminish and scaled profiles should become more alike if a round limit emerges.
finding: The shape records compare ant ensembles with rotor controls and reveal why radius, boundary width and accumulated visit density need separate measurements.
caveat: A finite collection of rescaled pictures cannot establish a unique limit shape. Rare breakouts can dominate ensemble moments.

title: A field guide to the shapes ants leave behind
question: How different can the visited territories look when the only instruction is a repeating string of left and right turns?
hypothesis: This is a visual reference collection rather than a separate hypothesis test: selected snapshots let readers connect rule strings with spatial outcomes.
finding: The archive preserves examples ranging from compact territories to structured builders, used as context for quantitative studies.
caveat: The examples are selected, not representative frequencies. Shape in a still image cannot certify an eventual growth regime.

title: A small home inside a growing territory
question: How can an ant keep returning to a small neighbourhood while its visited region continues to grow?
hypothesis: Positional spread and time near home should distinguish confinement from the total extent of accumulated exploration.
finding: The saved home and spread measurements provide the descriptive starting point for the tether programme.
caveat: Confinement depends on the observation window and home definition. A growing historical footprint does not directly measure where the ant currently spends time.

title: Which rules keep an ant close to home?
question: Is tethering an isolated curiosity, or a recurring kind of behaviour among very slow-growing rules?
hypothesis: Screening restarts on saved fields should identify repeatable confinement and possible families of home behaviour.
finding: The tether screen finds a broader collection for the later home-type and intervention studies, rather than relying on a single striking rule.
caveat: Restart position, heading and field age matter. A field that confines one restart may not confine another.

title: Can an early growth budget predict later territory?
question: Does a measured transport budget remain useful when we carry it forward to a later window instead of reconstructing the same window?
hypothesis: If the growth budget persists, a forecast fixed from earlier area information should predict later area better than a changing transient would allow.
finding: The saved forecast evaluates persistence of the growth budget using area endpoints.
caveat: This does not independently identify the boundary-entry and occupation factors: the budget can be reconstructed from area itself.

title: Rechecking roughness with the right size variable
question: Are comparisons of boundary-width exponents robust to fitting against radius rather than clock time?
hypothesis: Refitting existing trajectories and checking related controls can expose apparent exponent gaps caused by growth rate or geometry.
finding: The reanalysis qualifies the earlier width comparisons and keeps radius-based and time-based claims distinct.
caveat: Changing the horizontal axis is not a new simulation or independent replication. It also does not remove persistent-shape contributions.

title: Does a crust at the edge control boundary occupation?
question: Some territories look as though they have a distinct outer layer. Does that visible structure predict how much time the ant spends near fresh ground?
hypothesis: Comparing selected crust-like and other rules can test whether that grouping organizes boundary occupation and interior motion.
finding: The saved comparison measures kappa and a displacement statistic across the selected rules.
caveat: A visually selected grouping is exploratory. It needs independent validation before being treated as a predictive mechanism.

title: Do thin turmites have the same visit profile as compact ants?
question: Can the radial visit-density argument be carried over to stateful walkers with square-root-like growth?
hypothesis: If the same uniform-occupation assumptions hold, the growth law should predict the accumulated profile.
finding: Several thin square-root walkers escape the board before a usable profile is obtained. Missing profiles cannot count as support for the formula.
caveat: Thin geometry and board censoring make this a different regime from a compact two-dimensional territory.

title: When does the cone-shaped visit profile stop working?
question: The accumulated cone follows under particular occupation and growth assumptions. Does it survive when noise changes a rotor’s growth law?
hypothesis: If only the exponent matters, a generalized profile formula should still predict noisy-rotor visit density.
finding: Away from the cube-root regime, occupation stops being sufficiently uniform and the proposed formula fails.
caveat: The failure rejects transfer of the assumptions; it does not invalidate the conditional derivation in the regime where those assumptions hold.

title: Pushing the perimeter question to much longer times
question: Do ant perimeters approach square-root-of-area scaling, or retain a genuinely different exponent from the rotor?
hypothesis: Extending selected trajectories to 2^36 steps should distinguish continued drift toward one half from a persistent excess.
finding: Both registered decision rules remain inconclusive. At the final window the ants no longer sit clearly above the rotor.
caveat: A very long trajectory still supplies only a few late windows. An inconclusive result is not confirmation of either limiting exponent.

title: Is the broad edge rough coastline or internal holes?
question: Surface cells include the rims of holes inside the territory. Could those holes explain the ant’s broader boundary compared with the rotor?
hypothesis: Removing internal-hole rims should remove the excess width if porosity, rather than the outer coastline, causes it.
finding: The excess remains on the outer interface. The hole explanation fails; the ant’s outer boundary itself carries the broader fluctuations.
caveat: The outermost-radius estimator misses overhangs, and the connectivity convention matters. This still mixes persistent shape with local roughness.

title: Does boundary occupation differ beyond territory size?
question: Boundary occupation and territory area are tied by growth. Is there a rule-specific difference left when similarly sized territories are compared?
hypothesis: A real rule effect should remain after area adjustment, and might track the longest interior excursions relative to radius.
finding: Area adjustment weakens the rule effect, while matched comparisons retain an excursion-cutoff association. The registered combined decision is unresolved.
caveat: Matching observed area does not create a causal intervention. Seed noise and shared trajectories motivate the later independent-seed tests.

title: What do the longest trips away from the boundary tell us?
question: When an ant leaves the edge, how do its longest interior excursions relate to its eventual boundary occupation?
hypothesis: A larger extreme-excursion cutoff relative to territory radius should accompany lower boundary occupation.
finding: The descriptive negative association persists across the tested windows, but the controls do not support treating it as calibrated mechanistic evidence.
caveat: Excursion durations are not spatial chord lengths. Coarse quantile bins, unfinished excursions and selected rules limit interpretation.

title: Is the split between slow and compact growers arbitrary?
question: The census separates very slow rules from a broad compact-growth peak. Does the headline exponent depend on exactly where we draw the cut?
hypothesis: If the compact-growth peak is robust, reasonable cut changes should leave its centre nearly unchanged.
finding: The central compact-growth estimate moves little across tested cuts, but the strict registered tolerance fails. The density trough is not exactly at the original cut.
caveat: Robustness of a summary does not establish a sharp physical phase transition.

title: Does the edge model beat a simple lookup table?
question: A model relating turning bias to fresh-ground entry looks predictive. Does it explain more than a few early rule letters already tell us?
hypothesis: A useful mechanistic predictor should outperform coarse letter-group baselines on rules held out of training.
finding: The chirality model beats one-letter grouping, but a three-letter lookup predicts more accurately. Its apparent success does not isolate a mechanism.
caveat: The original quoted score confused correlation with predictive R-squared. Bootstrap intervals condition on the fitted models and omit training and seed uncertainty.

title: Long interior trips, with territory size fixed by design
question: Does the connection between extreme interior excursions and boundary occupation survive comparing ants at the same visited area?
hypothesis: Excursion-tail information measured on separate seeds should improve prediction beyond boundary residence and perimeter geometry.
finding: The larger-area association and held-out predictive improvement persist. The primary small-area correlation criterion fails; a narrower-band sensitivity does not erase that failure.
caveat: This selected cohort supports an association, not causality. Full all-seed thread replay was not performed, and an earlier noise-floor failure remains.

title: Persistent shape or genuinely rough coastline?
question: The ant’s outer edge is broader than the rotor’s. Is that a slowly changing large-scale shape, or shorter-wavelength roughening?
hypothesis: Separating low and high angular modes, with radius-matched controls, should distinguish those explanations.
finding: Calibration and a bounded pilot validate acquisition and expose sparse angular bins. The full scientific comparison remains pending.
caveat: The pilot is too small for the registered control count. It cannot decide between the competing roughness explanations.

title: Matching size without reusing the same trajectory
question: Could the excursion-cutoff association be an artefact of estimating area and both compared quantities from the same ant runs?
hypothesis: Splitting seeds into independent roles should preserve the association if shared-trajectory noise is not its whole explanation.
finding: The registered concordance and interval criteria hold at both tested windows after separating the seed roles.
caveat: This reuses selected rules, rather than validating on new ones. Noisy area matching, escape exclusions and the earlier reliability failure remain limitations.

title: Does the excursion link survive a rule-level model?
question: Matched pairs suggest a relationship between extreme excursions and boundary occupation. Does a split-seed model find it across whole rules?
hypothesis: An area-adjusted occupation residual should predict the excursion cutoff in independent seed halves.
finding: The main registered association and prediction criteria fail. The sign stays negative, but the effect is weaker and less stable than predicted; exploratory subsets cannot rescue that verdict.
caveat: The Gaussian constant-variance model is inadequate for the heavy-tailed response, and a puzzling pooled slope remains undiagnosed. These failures constrain any mechanistic reading.

title: Does a maturing colour field change return behaviour?
question: Might the age and visit history of cells explain why ants differ in returning from the interior to the edge?
hypothesis: Age-resolved measurements could connect return hazards to field maturation rather than to a rule label alone.
finding: The work establishes an instrument and prospective feasibility pilot. Scientific confirmation has not been run.
caveat: Feasibility is not confirmation. Age and colour-phase measurements remain observational, and unfinished excursions need explicit treatment.

title: Do early rule letters control launches from the edge?
question: Changing an early letter often has a larger effect than changing a late one. Does that happen because the boundary mostly exposes early colours?
hypothesis: Changes in boundary launch rates should predict changes in occupation across controlled rule mutations.
finding: The confirmation does not establish the launch-rate mechanism: key held-out prediction criteria fail, while a position gradient and mixed signs persist.
caveat: Only a small validation set is informative and early mutations also change retention. The mechanism remains unresolved rather than cleanly ruled out.

title: Are there special gates between the edge and interior?
question: Could a few directional crossing patterns explain why some ants spend more time at the boundary?
hypothesis: Gate summaries should improve held-out prediction beyond the registered baseline before an intervention stage is justified.
finding: The gate features do not establish the required added predictive value. The baseline already captures much of the occupation budget; the intervention stage was not run.
caveat: Some gate reliability and absolute-control checks fail. A strong baseline built from related occupation quantities can also make the test close to an accounting comparison.

title: Can rare long absences explain boundary occupation?
question: An ant can spend most of its time away from the edge in a small number of long interior episodes. Is that tail budget the missing explanation?
hypothesis: Separating episode rates from duration tails can test whether rare absences account for rule differences in boundary time.
finding: Confirmation passes its coverage gates, but the added-prediction criterion fails at the smaller area. The later occupation forecast passes its error threshold, although simple persistence predicts better.
caveat: The tail decomposition is largely forced by time-budget accounting, so its large contribution is not causal evidence. The parametric tail family fails calibration and is retained only as a sensitivity.

title: What is already known about ants and rotor walkers?
question: Which published results genuinely constrain our growth and boundary questions, and which similarities are only analogies?
hypothesis: This documentary review separates established statements about specific models from proposed transfers to generalised Langton’s ants.
finding: The review records source access, claim locators and distinctions among displacement, visited range, width and local time.
caveat: Abstract-only and inaccessible sources cannot establish technical details. A rotor theorem does not automatically apply to heading-relative ant dynamics.

title: Running thousands of ants without changing the answer
question: Can a graphics processor accelerate a large census while returning exactly the CPU’s classifications and end-state statistics?
hypothesis: Many independent, long ant trajectories should fill GPU lanes efficiently, provided every output agrees with the CPU oracle.
finding: The compared CSVs are byte-identical. The recorded large census workload runs several times faster than the six-thread CPU baseline.
caveat: The timing sample is small and hardware-specific. A single serial ant does not gain that batch speedup, and short jobs have substantial overhead.

title: Faster growth measurements, checked byte for byte
question: Can the GPU produce the same full growth and shape measurements as the CPU probe for large batches of rules and seeds?
hypothesis: The port should preserve every CSV byte while speeding up stepping-heavy independent trajectories.
finding: Equivalence checks pass. A fresh-build remeasurement supersedes the original stale-binary benchmark and gives a roughly four-to-sixfold gain on the recorded workload.
caveat: The CPU baseline shifted substantially for an unexplained reason. The timings are few runs on one GPU, not a general performance guarantee.

title: Does the opening-run effect survive a different growth clock?
question: A rule’s initial run of identical letters predicts boundary occupation after area adjustment. Does using current rather than early area change that association?
hypothesis: Matched rule families with fixed composition should retain a positive effect if early-area conditioning is not creating it.
finding: The support gate fails: too few complete families survive. The registered effects are therefore not fitted or scored.
caveat: Differential retention is the result here, not evidence for or against the effect. Lowering the gate after the run would change the test.

title: Does an ant’s opening instruction predict its boundary time?
question: A longer opening run of identical turns appears linked to boundary occupation after adjusting for area. Does it replicate on fresh rules, and does changing one letter reproduce it?
hypothesis: Fresh-rule prediction and paired mutations can distinguish a repeatable association from an apparently causal effect of opening-run length.
finding: The conditional association replicates, but mutation effects are asymmetric. Later fresh-ground analysis shows why conditioning on area can create much of the apparent direct occupation effect.
caveat: Letter direction, composition, regime selection and growth are intertwined. The replicated conditional association is not a causal estimate.

title: A loop intervention that was deliberately not run
question: If short square loops keep an ant near the edge, would suppressing those loops change its boundary occupation?
hypothesis: Targeted loop suppression should have a larger effect than matched-rate noise, but only after the parent loop experiment passes its gate.
finding: The parent’s required mediation test fails, so this follow-up closes without running. The folder is a plan, with no intervention data.
caveat: There is no experimental result for loop surgery. Keeping the unrun test visible prevents a proposed mechanism from looking like established evidence.

title: What information is hidden in the start of the rule?
question: Short prefixes predict boundary occupation surprisingly well. Which simple feature of the prefix is carrying that information?
hypothesis: Decoding prefix features may reveal a compact predictive description, especially the opening run of identical turns.
finding: The exploratory decode identifies opening-run length as a candidate and motivates a fresh-rule replication rather than treating the discovery score as confirmation.
caveat: This is post hoc feature discovery. Predictive success can reflect territory size and selection as well as direct boundary dynamics.

title: The square-loop explanation that failed its test
question: Long opening runs can make an ant circle small squares on young cells. Does that explain their apparent boundary-occupation effect?
hypothesis: Interior loop frequency should mediate the association strongly enough to pass a registered reduction and reliability test.
finding: The deciding mediation prediction fails. The attractive square-loop account is not established, and its proposed intervention follow-up is not launched.
caveat: Loops can still occur without being the proposed mediator. This cohort was already used to discover the association, so it is not an independent replication.

title: What would uniform occupation actually predict?
question: We normalize boundary time by perimeter divided by area. Should a walker that is uniformly spread over a growing territory therefore have kappa equal to one?
hypothesis: Because the probe averages over an expanding time window, the uniform reference must account for growth within that window.
finding: The corrected reference differs from one. This changes the baseline against which the ant’s boundary occupation should be compared.
caveat: The calculation is conditional on the assumed growth and geometry. A deviation from the reference does not by itself identify a return mechanism.

title: Why does a longer opening run make fresh ground harder to enter?
question: The number of boundary steps needed to discover a new cell is nearly linear in the rule’s opening-run length. Where does that law come from?
hypothesis: Young boundary colours might supply a local fresh-ground mechanism, testable by tracing entries, changing the interior and adding background colour.
finding: The fresh-ground relation predicts well, but a simple isolated-edge account is incomplete. The later analysis reproduces the earlier fixed-area occupation effect through conditioning, without requiring a direct effect on kappa.
caveat: Some high-background predictions become untestable because ants leave the board. Mutations change letter direction as well as run length, so no isolated causal claim about kappa follows.

title: The opening run predicts entry, not simply occupation
question: Does the start of the rule control boundary time directly, or primarily the chance of stepping onto fresh ground?
hypothesis: Comparing rotations of the same rule and fresh-rule predictions can distinguish a cyclic rule property from a fresh-ground effect.
finding: The cyclic-necklace explanation fails, while opening-run length predicts the inverse fresh-ground entry probability on held-out fresh rules.
caveat: The intercept and slope still need an explanation. Discovery stages reused inspected data, and the unrun stage must not be counted as evidence.

title: Is the ant unusual against the right comparison?
question: Ant boundary occupation sits below a simple uniform reference. Do rotor and random walkers also deviate when each gets its own growth-adjusted reference?
hypothesis: A fair comparison must use each walker’s measured growth and perimeter scaling rather than giving all walkers the ant’s baseline.
finding: Every tested comparison walker stays above its reference, while the typical census ant sits below. Small rotor noise produces an occupation overshoot; the predicted monotone response and small-noise growth robustness both fail.
caveat: The reference assumes usable power-law windows. Escapes force shorter noisy-walker windows, several rows are nonstationary, and ant single-run variation differs from walker between-seed uncertainty.

title: How do ants draw diagonal crystal lattices?
question: Some rules leave remarkably long diagonal rays. Are these self-sustaining travelling paths, repeated reversals or structures launched by a local spinner?
hypothesis: Ray segmentation, local-patch tests and planned transplants can discriminate those candidate causes rather than identifying a mechanism from appearance alone.
finding: Calibration and several anatomy stages are complete, including local-patch and ray-structure tests. The programme remains partial; key ray-end and transplant interventions have not all run.
caveat: The striking pictures are selected deterministic trajectories. A visible periodic motif is not enough to establish a self-sustaining highway.

title: Which part of a rule controls access to fresh ground?
question: Rules with similar growth exponents still differ in time spent at the boundary. Can we predict that difference from the instructions themselves?
hypothesis: Prefix prediction, colour accounting and single-letter mutations can identify whether early rule positions carry transferable information.
finding: Several stages find predictive prefix structure and stronger effects from early mutations, motivating the later opening-run studies. The programme is only partly complete.
caveat: Growth and area conditioning can create apparent occupation effects. Later mechanism work limits causal readings of this earlier predictive programme.

title: How much of the spread of kappa is accounted for?
question: Boundary occupation varies a lot between rules. How much of that variance is start-to-start noise, how much can the rule opening predict, and how much is left?
hypothesis: A post hoc budget from earlier committed results can split the variance without new runs (not a registered test).
finding: About 0.15 of the variance is start noise, 0.47-0.54 is predicted by the first eight letters and 0.31-0.38 is rule-determined but unexplained.
caveat: Three different cohorts feed the budget, no uncertainty is propagated (shares are rough to +-0.1), and the location of the kappa distribution is not addressed.

title: Is the predictive part of the rule at its start?
question: Is the information about kappa specific to the first letters of a rule, or would the last letters or simple letter counts do as well?
hypothesis: Registered: the first eight letters predict held-out kappa well (within 0.1 of an earlier 0.63); the last eight and composition do not.
finding: All four registered predictions held: held-out R^2 is +0.62 for the first eight letters, -0.11 for the last eight and +0.08 for composition, which adds nothing to the prefix.
caveat: The prefix lookup is a family-membership predictor and families overlap between training and test; the unexplained third of the spread is not reached.

title: Does the lead alone carry the prefix signal?
question: Which part of the opening carries the prefix information: the lead, or the run structure of the first few runs?
hypothesis: Registered: the lead alone reaches R^2 of at least 0.15, two runs reach 0.40, and three runs come within 0.10 of the eight-letter prefix.
finding: Three of four predictions failed: the lead alone scores about 0 and the first two, three and four runs reach 0.25, 0.34 and 0.48 against 0.62 for eight letters.
caveat: Run keys and letter-prefix keys differ in granularity and no group-count control was run; the result is unconditional, unlike the earlier fixed-area lead association.

title: Which letters of the opening carry the kappa signal?
question: The first eight letters of a rule predict held-out kappa. Is the information in a few early letters, or spread across them?
hypothesis: Registered: position 1 carries nothing, positions 2-4 each carry at least 0.05 of R^2, and positions 5-8 carry no more than the largest of positions 2-4.
finding: Three of four predictions held and one failed: position 5 carries the most (loss 0.40), positions 2-7 each cost 0.2-0.4, and position 8 costs 0.07.
caveat: The lookup is a conjunctive key, so a large loss at a position means it matters jointly with the others; main effects and interactions are not separated.

title: Does the edge-entry law survive a different lattice?
question: The square-lattice opening-run law leaves its constants unexplained. Do changing loop length and neighbour count distinguish what sets them?
hypothesis: Registered hexagonal and triangular-cell comparisons test loop-length scaling and occupation against a lattice-specific uniform reference.
finding: Registered plan only; no lattice measurements have been run at registration.
caveat: The predictions are prospective. Growth, support and calibration gates must pass before interpreting the proposed comparisons.

title: Is the prefix signal additive over letters or does it need interactions?
question: The eight-letter lookup carries information spread over letters 2-7. Would a model that adds up one effect per letter position do as well?
hypothesis: Registered before the run: an additive model scores below 0.40 held-out R^2, a model with pairwise interactions reaches at least 0.50, and the full lookup beats the additive model by at least 0.15.
finding: Two of three registered predictions held and one failed: an additive model scores 0.11 held-out R^2, adding all pairwise interactions gives 0.35 (predicted at least 0.50), and the full eight-letter lookup scores 0.62.
caveat: The ridge penalty was not tuned and only binary indicators were used; the lookup also exploits prefix families shared between training and test, so interaction structure and family membership are not separated.

title: Does the prefix signal survive unseen rule families?
question: The eight-letter prefix predicts held-out kappa. Is that a transferable letter-level rule, or do rules sharing an opening simply behave alike?
hypothesis: Registered: the lookup works on seen families but collapses on unseen ones (confirmed), while a pairwise-interaction model keeps its signal across families and beats the lookup there (both failed).
finding: With whole 6-letter prefix families held out, every model falls below the training mean: the lookup goes from 0.59 to -0.16 and the pairwise model from 0.30 to -0.69.
caveat: Only 43 uneven families and about five held out per fold, so held-out family means differ from the training mean; this does not show that no structure exists within a family.

title: Why do some rules paint a plateau with diagonal rectangles?
question: One rule (RLLLLLLLRRLRR) leaves most cells visited exactly twice and draws nested 45-degree rectangles. What property of a rule produces that, and is it a different growth class?
hypothesis: Registered before the follow-up steps: the rule grows with area exponent at least 0.9 (not the 2/3 of the chaotic rules), and the pattern is set by the early letters so that flipping a late letter keeps the plateau.
finding: The first prediction held: area grows roughly in proportion to time (exponent 0.995) and width roughly as the square root of time (0.498), a diffusive class. The second was falsified: none of ten late-letter flips keeps the plateau, so the family is fragile and the late letters matter.
caveat: This guide summarises only the early steps of the README (growth class and ablation); the census and later steps are not summarised here. The fit window was moved after seeing per-octave data, which the README states as a post hoc choice.

title: Where does the lead slope live?
question: Does circulation frequency explain why the birth-cost slope falls with loop length?
hypothesis: The lattice slope difference might be carried by circulation episodes per birth rather than reads per circulation.
finding: The registered circulation decomposition fails. Its headline frequency comparison counts interior loops and is not interpretable as evidence; boundary-only segmentation is the next proposal.
caveat: Per-colour survival patterns are exploratory. A formally passing statistic with an interior-contaminated estimator does not validate the mechanism.

title: Where on the edge is the ant's missing boundary time?
question: Ants spend less time on boundary cells than a uniform walker would. Is the shortfall on flat stretches of edge, or on exposed corners, bays and tips?
hypothesis: Registered: ants return to flat-edge cells more, relative to their share, than to exposed cells (median ratio Q at least 1.18, above 1 for at least three quarters of rules), and rougher edges mean a larger deficit.
finding: The deficit survives a measure that needs no uniform reference (ants 0.87 of uniform, rotor 1.80, random walk 1.31), and the old kappa/1.105 tracks it rule by rule to roughly 7-9%. The exposure prediction failed: Q is above 1 for only 64% of rules (95% interval 52-75%), and the rotor and random walk lean the same way. The second prediction depended on the first and was not scored. A review found that the after-the-fact flat-edge reading is mostly class composition: compared with the rotor, the ant is short on both kinds of edge, and about half the gap is birth steps.
caveat: One cohort of 64 rules up to 2^26 steps. Exposure is entangled with cell age, colour and depth, which were not recorded. The flat-edge reading and the review are post hoc. Three board-filling patched runs were excluded only in a sensitivity check.

title: Can the column sweeper be proved to run forever?
question: RLRLLL switches to a column sweeper after about 12.7 billion steps. Is there a finite family of configurations the rule maps into itself for every column height?
hypothesis: The sweeper is a three-phase macro-transition with an exactly affine cycle clock, constant growth and bounded reach, so one finite check covers every height.
finding: All five registered predictions held on 4,729 cycles. A separate checker closes the family for every even bulk height (cycle length 12m plus 934, 1058 or 898); the law reproduces every measured cycle and implies the squared distance per step tends to 3/4.
caveat: The base case is one uncertified long simulation and the checker is unverified Rust, tested by brute force and negative controls. It certifies without explaining, and the trigger inside the blob is unknown.

title: Is there a compact boundary state?
question: When the ant leaves the boundary, how far out does the colour field decide where and when it next returns?
hypothesis: No bounded-radius summary suffices: the relevant colour field extends over a fixed fraction of the territory scale (P1), with a compact-state alternative registered alongside (P1-alt).
finding: For the typical short excursion a compact state exists: median reach 0.05 to 0.10 of the territory scale and barely growing with it, so P1 is falsified and P1-alt met. Weighted by interior time the reach is of order the territory scale and grows roughly linearly with it. Controls passed (the random-walk control in the pilot only).
caveat: A within-depth shuffle cannot separate specific colours from spatial structure. The time-weighted prediction was informed by the pilot. The deep/shallow split conditions on an outcome. Tethered, crystal and log-growing rules were not in the cohort.

title: What does the late switch look like?
question: Can one picture show RLRLLL's whole territory through its switch from blob to column sweeper?
hypothesis: A visualisation, with no prediction registered. Pre-run consistency checks against the archived trajectory were written down first.
finding: After 12.7 billion steps the blob covers 9.5 million cells. In the next 0.30 billion steps (2.3% of the run) the sweeper lays a wedge reaching 7.8 times as many new cells, until the ant meets the edge of a 32,768² board. The exit step matches the archived trace exactly.
caveat: One deterministic trajectory, cut off by the board. The colour resolution is the snapshot spacing, and the blob's colour ramp is a display choice. The picture does not explain what triggers the switch.

title: What must the grid hold for a highway to start?
question: Every census highway starts after a chaotic phase. Which cells of the old pattern does the highway actually need, and do different rules need the same thing?
hypothesis: Registered before measuring: the cells the future depends on collapse near onset (P1); the seed is a highway fragment plus a few cells (P2); it sits at the edge facing out (P3); rules building the same highway share a seed (P4); bigger seeds mean later onsets (P5). A follow-up registered single-cell knock-outs of the seed (Q1-Q3).
finding: The set of cells the future will read drops from thousands to the size of the highway trail about a tenth of a period before onset. Just before onset the seed is that trail plus a median of 3 cells in all 406 independent onsets, and about a quarter of a period later the ant is heading away from its territory in 402 of them; alone on a blank board it reproduces the highway exactly (566 of 566). P1 and P3 held, P2 held trivially, P4 held only within families of rules sharing a long prefix, and P5 failed. No single cell triggers the launch; about half the seed cells matter.
caveat: Rules sharing a prefix are merged into independent events, but families still weigh heavily. The links of onset time to highway size and to seed fragility were found after the data were seen and are not tested. The seed is the smallest set of cells the future was seen to depend on, which is enough to reproduce it but not shown to be necessary. Only onsets up to one billion steps are covered.

title: Were the late highways real?
question: Many highways reported after a billion steps were axis-aligned with onsets near multiples of 2 to the 31. Are they highways, or artefacts of the 32768-cell board?
hypothesis: Registered before running: these rules fill the whole board, so their escape time grows with the board area (B1). A second registration predicted that at least 24 of the 26 remaining late highways reproduce on a board twice as wide (B2).
finding: They are board fillers: on boards of 1024, 2048 and 4096 cells the same rules escape four times later for each doubling and visit 99% of the board first. Of the 54 reported late highways, 25 are fillers and one is a ray cut off by the board edge. All 26 other late highways re-run on a 65536-cell board reproduce their onset exactly, so the second prediction held. Corrected yields are 2.0% of surviving rules in the decade to ten billion steps and 1.6% in the next, so the earlier finding of a thinning tail is withdrawn.
caveat: B1 failed its own 1% tolerance at small boards because of a perimeter term, though the scaling is clear. The filler filter was chosen after seeing the footprints. The earlier sweeps have not had the board-size check, and three decades of a dozen or so events each cannot rule out a slow decline.

title: What does the transport evidence establish?
question: Which boundary occupation, return and regime claims survive their corrections?
hypothesis: Editorial consolidation only; no new scientific prediction.
finding: Eleven scoped records separate accounting, prediction, intervention and instrument outcomes, with pinned evidence and queryable JSON.
caveat: Not exhaustive; gate eligibility remains unknown and no mechanism or universal classification is established.

title: Can we attack a claim instead of just running it longer?
question: Can an automated loop that perturbs starts, places obstacles, and searches adaptively find counterexamples to claims like 'this rule is chaotic' or 'this rule forms this highway' that a longer blank-board run would miss?
hypothesis: A claim about every start can be tested by trying hard to break it, and the result will say Falsified, Survived, Unsupported or Invalid rather than a bare yes.
finding: Five registered claims, about 545 attacks each. RRRL's highway type depends on the start (a six-cell patch suffices); RRLR is falsified, and only its blank start is late. RL, RRL and RLL survived every attack. Of seven predictions, P1, P4 and P5 held; P2, P3, P6 and P7 were wrong in whole or in part. A clean rerun with the improved search kept every verdict.
caveat: Survived means no counterexample in these attack classes at this horizon, never a proof. Dense random backgrounds, larger patches and growth-exponent claims are untested. The first pooled Clopper-Pearson interval was withdrawn because adaptive candidates are correlated.

title: Why did the adversary lose to random sampling?
question: The harness's adaptive attacker lost to 64 random patches on three of three highway claims. Was hill-climbing the wrong tool, or was this climber badly built?
hypothesis: An evolutionary search that seeds from the random draws, keeps elites, mutates at several scales and treats the obstacle as a gene will find longer escape delays than random search at the same budget.
finding: On the delay objective the new search beats random sampling on RL (p about 1e-5 to 1e-8) and RRL (p about 1e-3), 30 replicates of 200 evaluations. As a counterexample finder it does not: on RRRL it found a different highway in 22 of 30 replicates, and 27 of 30 with immigration, against 30 of 30 for plain random draws. Two of the four round-one predictions failed in the direction that matters (E1 and E4).
caveat: One sampler, three rules, one budget. The chaotic-claim objective is still an unvalidated heuristic. The adaptive search is stronger at hunting long transients, not at falsification.

title: Which exact bookkeeping laws can an ant never break?
question: Which weighted sums of position, heading, time and cell colours, modulo 2 or 4, are unchanged by every local move of an ant, for any starting field?
hypothesis: The miner will recover checkerboard parity, heading parity and the colour-clock balance, and will say nothing about growth or highways.
finding: A registered, exhaustive search over a small linear ansatz, with every candidate checked against all local transitions. Each law it reports is a proof by induction. Its output feeds the stage-2 experiment, which found that these laws depend only on the colour count and net turn.
caveat: Completeness holds only inside the ansatz at moduli 2 and 4. Nonlinear, edge-flux, spatially weighted and history-dependent invariants are not searched. The constraints do not imply the cube-root exponent, trapping or highway formation, and no family is pruned.

title: Do exact conservation laws know the order of the colours?
question: For an n-colour ant, what is the full group of additive local conservation laws at every modulus, and does it carry information about the rule beyond its colour count and number of R turns?
hypothesis: The law group depends only on the colour count and the net turn, so it cannot separate rules that differ only in the order of their colours.
finding: Held on all 508 rules of length up to 8 and four families: no rule-specific content, and 0 mismatches against the independent enumerative miner. One prediction (P4) was falsified as registered: a pure-tape heading law exists for every even n, not only some. All 582 confirmed highway rules share the same tile-free law group. What separates chaos from highways lies outside additive local laws.
caveat: Exhaustive only for n up to 8, with an oracle for n up to 6. The extension to all n rests on a derivation, not a checked proof. Non-additive families (pair potentials, edge flux, history) are not tested, so the pruning signature defers only re-mining these families.

title: Do single cells act as gates on long excursions?
question: In the long journeys an ant makes through the interior, do the cells it reads most act as gates, so that changing one of them changes the return time or the reach more than changing a matched ordinary cell?
hypothesis: Traffic-selected candidate cells will change the log return time by at least 0.25 more than matched controls, and the reach by at least 10% more, each with a rule-cluster bootstrap interval above zero.
finding: Neither registered prediction was met. On 3 rules, 260 departures and 617 matched pairs, candidates differ from matched cells by -0.05 in mean absolute log2 return time (95% interval -0.41 to 0.29) and by +0.10 in relative reach (-0.11 to 0.30). Single cells often change outcomes, but busy cells have no resolved advantage over matched ones. Rule heterogeneity is large.
caveat: Only three rules, selected conditional on long durations, so this is a candidate-ranking result and not a family-wide exclusion of sparse gates. Reach is censored at the cap, and the sampler silently skips episodes whose undo log overflows, so eligibility is unknown.

title: Do the census highways survive a check on the whole configuration?
question: A highway claim has so far rested on a repeating trace. Can a check on the configuration itself, with the ant in a window and blank cells ahead of it, certify that the pattern reproduces itself for all future periods?
hypothesis: A translated-cycler certificate exists for the census highways, and it fails for chaotic and non-highway controls.
finding: 571 of 571 census highways certified (568 at the first snapshot tried), with the controls passing and the plain loop identical to the reference ant from step 0 for the 408 rules with onset up to 3e5. The soundness of the certificate is a Lean theorem for an arbitrary rule and every number of periods, so each result is an instance of a machine-checked statement.
caveat: The four instance clauses are computed by a Python program, not replayed in Lean. The Lean ant is a transcription of the rule, validated against the Rust ant only by comparison. The certificate covers the future from the snapshot; how a blank board reaches it is plain simulation. A failure would not mean not a highway. Not attacked with the falsification harness.

title: Are the other three census escapes sweepers too?
