question: The census lists RLLLLRRL, RLLLRLRLLL and RLLLLRLRRL as escaping without a highway. Do they share the RLRLLL column sweeper's exact clock, so the proof machinery transfers?
hypothesis: Each target shows an exact affine clock in its revolution times, and a narrow-ribbon signature tracks that clock (predictions G1 to G6, registered before the runs).
finding: No: the three escapes are not three sweepers. RLLLRLRLLL has an exact clock for 29,854 consecutive revolutions, growing as a filled territory. RLLLLRRL fails the registered test but is exactly periodic with period 19 from step 1.47e10, about 2e9 steps after the census saw it escape. RLLLLRLRRL is still a blob at 6e10. G1, G3 and G4 failed as registered, and G2's onset prediction failed.
caveat: Board edges decided when the census runs stopped, not what the ants were. The period cap of 6 was too small and the 19 was found post hoc. Whether either spiral continues forever, what triggers the late onset, and why 19, are open. All classifications are blank-board and probe observations, none attacked with the falsification harness.

title: Can the ant stop paying for the whole board?
question: The lean sweeper allocates and clears a square board per worker, whatever the ant does. Does a tiled grid with sparse tiles, a bounded cache and compressed inactive tiles cut peak memory at an acceptable throughput cost?
hypothesis: Sparse allocation alone cuts memory where the footprint is small; bit-packing alone adds little for irregular patterns; a compression stage is needed to move memory on structured ones.
finding: Output is byte-identical to the dense backend in all 204 benchmark runs. Sparse tiles use 0.10 to 0.13 times the dense memory on compact patterns, and 12 MiB where dense needs 4.2 GiB on a 65536 board. LZ4 on packed tiles gave 0.19 times dense on one structured pattern. A small cache on a large footprint runs 20 to 40 times slower. Prediction P5 failed in direction, and the compression-ratio prediction D5 failed (about 100 times, not 15 to 60).
caveat: One machine, one build, a shared environment, single-thread runs and five census workloads. The structured-pattern compression result rests on a single rule. Dense throughput drifted up to 20% between batches, so ratios within 1.2 of 1 are noise. The default stays dense.

title: The same ant on a Mac GPU
question: Can native Metal execution preserve every census result from the CPU oracle?
hypothesis: Independent ants can share a GPU while each ant retains its serial update order.
finding: The new optional wgpu backend runs on Metal and passes its hardware oracle tests, including seeded backgrounds and pool retries.
caveat: This is an implementation and correctness record. macOS speedup has not been measured; CUDA probe statistics and the browser are separate instruments.

title: Why do some ants fill the plane at exactly 2(k+1) steps per cell?
question: The board fillers R^k L R R... cover any board at 2(k+1) steps per cell, and the census lists 304 square-filling builders. What mechanism sets that number, which rules share it, and are the builders one class?
hypothesis: A crawler made of 2x2 square loops walks along a three-row edge profile, reading each visit count 0..2k+1 once per cell, so every cell costs 2(k+1) visits and the rule must read R^k L R^(k+1) there; corners read count 2k+2 (predictions P1 to P6, registered before the runs).
finding: Yes for the edge: the crawler is proved for every k and checked for k up to 64. All 25 census board fillers run an exact revolution clock with slope 8(k+1), and a quadratic fitted on three small boards predicts every later board exit to the step, including the census records. Flipping only the corner letter breaks the ring, while rules that never fill from a blank board run a transplanted ring forever. In the census, 218 of 361 rules with the right turns are rings and rings are most of the builders, but the registered necessity test failed: other crawler families (a reversed table, two-visit spirals) fill at the same integer costs.
caveat: Only the straight edge is proved; the corner and the ring's persistence are observed, not proved. Which seeds reach the ring from a blank board is unexplained. The two-visit and reversed-table families are post hoc and only partly inspected. One window per rule at 2^27 steps.

title: The turn map hides a clock
question: Can two fields prescribe the same next turn everywhere but produce different boundary returns?
hypothesis: One-time colour shuffles that keep each cell’s next turn may retain much of the unrestricted shuffle effect.
finding: All 640 next-turn-preserving replays changed paths and return tuples; all 640 full-word shams matched. The stronger prediction failed in two of six comparisons, and 17 of 24 start/area groups failed minimum episode support.
caveat: Excluded pilot: three rules, four starts each, selected long excursions and large field edits. No censoring was observed. Sensitivity is not an occupation forecast or an information fraction; the mechanistic comparison remains unresolved.

title: Does CI check that the fast sweepers agree?
question: Most census data comes from sweep_lean, documented as identical to sweep, and from its tiled storage backend, documented as byte-identical to dense. The hosted reproducibility job checked neither. Can the small CI batch pin both down end to end through the command line?
hypothesis: Registered before running: sweep_lean matches sweep byte for byte (P1); it is identical at 1 and 3 threads, dense and tiled (P2); tiled storage under default and eviction-forcing stress settings matches dense (P3); and the new check can fail (P4).
finding: P1 to P3 held on 57 rules (lengths 2 to 6) at 32,768 steps on a 256-cell grid, 14 recorded runs. The stress settings really evicted (72,234 evictions) and used the storage paths they name. P4 held for the vacuity guard: a cache too large to evict makes the check fail. A first lz4 setting never evicted and would have passed vacuously; the script now asserts from grid statistics that each stress path is exercised.
caveat: An engineering identity check, not a measurement: it compares two fast paths with each other, not with the reference oracle, on one small batch, step budget, toolchain and machine. It says nothing about other budgets, grids, backgrounds, checkpoint/resume or longer rules. No genuine byte difference was injected, so P4 shows only the vacuity guard.

title: Does the exposure classifier count what its docs say?
question: Is the boundary-cell exposure class (number of unvisited 4-neighbours) used by the 2026-10-20 kappa exposure test computed exactly as documented and consistently with the probe?
hypothesis: An independent z3 checker, written from the docs, should accept the instrument's classes for every 3x3 pattern and visit order and reject mutated tables and specs.
finding: Held: 65/65 checks as expected. The Rust truth table equals the spec for all 512 patterns and 986,410 visit orders; incremental bookkeeping is proved inductive; replayed walks match the probe exactly; u = 4 never occurs (all 6,154 committed windows). Six negative controls rejected.
caveat: An instrument check, not a result about ants. Classes are exposure counts, not shapes: u = 2 includes one-cell strips and u = 1 includes T-junction cells, so the 2026-10-20 verdicts stand but its corner/flat wording is a loose reading.

title: Is the late-highway yield per decade flat?
question: Among rules that still look chaotic, does a fixed fraction find a highway in each decade of time, or does the yield fall? A fourth decade, (1e11, 1e12], was designed and power-checked.
hypothesis: Registered before any 1e12 run: an exact binomial test against a flat yield of 1.67% per decade, with the power table computed first. After the power analysis showed the test was weak, a flat hazard across the whole length <= 10 census was fitted from existing data instead, and about 12 highways among the 702 survivors were predicted for (1e11, 1e12].
finding: No 1e12 run was made: even all 702 survivors would have under 50% power against a halving per decade. From the existing census, the onset hazard per at-risk rule is flat to within about 8% per decade (factor 0.97 [0.91, 1.03] over 1e2 to 1e11), and the highway count per decade is close to constant, so onset times look log-uniform. Shared trajectories would save nothing.
caveat: Exploratory: the fit windows were chosen after seeing the table. Length <= 10 rules only, a finite and depleting pool, and older sweep boards never had the second-board check. The (1e11, 1e12] prediction is registered but un-run.

title: How long do rules that share a prefix share a trajectory?
question: Several notes treat rules with a common prefix as sharing dynamics for a while. Is there an exact statement of how long, provable for all rules, and what does it say about the census?
hypothesis: Two rules' positions agree exactly until the first read of the first colour where their turn tables differ (with a prefix and a periodic-lift variant). Registered expectations: that first-read time grows like a cube law in the colour, and equal late-highway onsets among prefix-sharing rules are explained by late first reads.
finding: z3 discharged all 75 proof obligations, and all 8 controls behaved as required after a repair. The statement held for every pair of rules up to length 6 against the reference ant. But first reads come early, within a few hundred steps for every survivor, so prefix-sharing rules separate within about 10^3 steps. The cube-law prediction (R2) failed. The equal late onsets (R4) are board fillers that share a fill rate, not shared trajectories.
caveat: z3 checks only the step obligations; the induction over steps is a pen proof, and no proof assistant was used. Positions only; the census findings cover length <= 10 survivors and the 25 fillers. No bound on first-read times is proved for all rules.

title: Do rotated rules build the same object?
question: Cyclic rotations of a rule share their bounding box far more often than chance among the 1e11 survivors. Is that shared structure, or only a shared size?
hypothesis: A rotated rule on a blank board is the original rule on a uniform background, so the question becomes background independence. Registered: footprint coincidences between backgrounds are common in the box-sharing classes and rare in matched controls, and do not persist.
finding: The identity held against an oracle. The box association is real but sits in about 10% of rotation classes, all small and bounded. Exact footprint coincidences are rare and come and go between decades. The coincidence-rate predictions failed as registered: both test and control had 2 of 8 classes, and the control ones are forced by mirror symmetry (a post hoc refinement). No class is background-independent, and for typical classes the background decides between bounded and escaping.
caveat: 8 test and 8 length-matched control classes, lengths 7 to 10, footprints only (colours and ant phase ignored), horizons 1e8 and 1e9 on a 2048 board, one representative per class. The 1e10 re-coincidence has no mechanism.

title: Is a chaotic edge a broken crawler?
question: The square-ring crawler, an ordered ant edge, has an exact birth cost of k + 5/4 boundary reads per new cell. Chaotic rules follow an empirical edge law, 1/c = 1.36 + 0.70 m in the opening run m. Does the crawler's accounting organise the chaotic edge's cost?
hypothesis: H-crawl: a chaotic edge is a fragmented crawler. Circulation around fresh 2x2 plaquettes breaks when a shared cell reads the wrong letter, so rules with the crawler's full turn table should approach the crawler line, and letters at positions m+1 to 2m+1 should matter most, in a window that moves with m (P0 to P3 registered before any run; a fresh-rule slope test, Stage 2, registered before its run).
finding: The crawler's cost is now an exact calibration point: 1/c = k + 5/4 in exact rationals, reproduced by the edge tracer to 0.002 on all 25 census fillers. Chaotic blobs with the crawler's table sit about 65% of the way from the lead law to the crawler line, against 15% for composition-matched controls, and only 6 of 129 such rules exceed the line, so it works as a ceiling. The positional story failed: near letters matter more than far ones, but there is no window that moves with m, and a single added same-turn letter more often lowers the cost. On fresh rules the steeper lead slope is matched by composition, and the fitted K3 kernel already predicts these rules at m up to 4.
caveat: Single blank-board start per rule; tracer horizon 2^24 on a 4096 board. Two thirds of fresh crawler-table rules became filler-like and were filtered out, so the kept rules are selected. Three census rules were seen in exploration (results unchanged without them). The K3 comparison is post hoc. The slope test's paired subset is small, so its failure is inconclusive rather than a dead end.

title: Does the cube root come from the repelling fresh ground or from the ant's memory?
question: Every canonical ant turns R on a blank cell, and inside its territory its colour field remembers past visits. Which of the two keeps the territory compact with area growing as t^(2/3)?
hypothesis: Splitting turn noise by cell type separates them: randomising turns only on fresh cells removes the wall, only on revisited cells removes the memory (the hybrid walker). Registered prior: memory carries the exponent, so the ant stays compact without the wall and the hybrid is porous.
finding: The prior failed. With memory kept and the first-departure turn randomised, the condition means of all six drawn core-class rules became porous (area exponent 0.86 to 0.91, near the memoryless walker's 0.93; 39 of 48 runs individually meet the thresholds). The hybrid walker, with the forced fresh-ground turn and a memoryless interior, has 0.73 at k = 24..30 and 0.72 at k = 27..31 against the rotor's 0.68: a finite-window separation. Ten per cent noise shifted the exponent by +0.03 (fresh cells) to +0.05 (revisits) but left the fresh-noise conditions compact.
caveat: Six rules from one class, 8 seeds each, finite windows. The hybrid's reading sits 0.002 over its registered threshold with an unresolved trend, so whether the wall alone eventually gives a cube root is open. Nothing here derives the exponent.

title: Can excursion-duration shape tell diffusive mixing from sweeping?
question: Does the shape of interior excursion durations collapse in tau/L or tau/L^2, separating a diffusive mixer from a sweeper when the mean alone cannot?
hypothesis: A nonparametric collapse Score with a fixed margin, calibrated so random walk prefers L^2 and mean-field prefers L, should discriminate before any ant reading.
finding: Stage one stopped: mean-field passed; random walk never grew L. Revision 1 reflecting cup grew L but failed compactness and Score preferred sweep scaling (frontier trapping); C1' inadequate; confirmation not run; cup-as-D design retired. Revision 2: Eden-style growth and internal DLA both passed compactness, yet Score preferred sweep scaling or neither; no calibrator passed, so confirmation was not run and both were retired for this Score.
caveat: Frozen C1/C1'/C2 stop gates; evolving probe boundary; right-censored opens. Development trajectories permanently excluded. Stay-on-reject cup retired as D calibrator; do not P-shop. Filled compact-domain candidate required before confirmation. The number-weighted Score is dominated by short boundary returns that do not scale with L, so it cannot certify diffusion even in compact walkers; this is an instrument limit, not an ant result.
